intro: Mottisfont, a National Trust estate in the Test valley near Romsey, has one tree on this map, and it is a big one. The Great Plane of Mottisfont stands close to a house that began as an Augustinian priory in the early 13th century, and Wikipedia calls it the largest London plane in Britain. OpenStreetMap records it at about 30 metres tall. Its age has not been confirmed. Entry is paid, free to Trust members, and the nearest station is Dunbridge, about 1.5 kilometres away.

question_answer: The largest London plane in Britain, according to Wikipedia, is the Great Plane of Mottisfont, on the National Trust's Mottisfont estate near Romsey in Hampshire. OpenStreetMap records it at about 30 metres tall. It stands close to the house, inside the paid estate, about 1.5 kilometres from Dunbridge station.
question_context: Most people meet London planes as street trees, a row of trunks along a pavement. The Great Plane of Mottisfont is what one becomes with a whole estate to itself. It grows beside a house in the Test valley that was founded as an Augustinian priory in the early 13th century and turned into a country house after Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries, now looked after by the National Trust. Wikipedia names it the largest London plane in Britain, and OpenStreetMap maps it by name as a landmark about 30 metres tall. Tree recorders have reported a greater height, a much larger girth and a planting in the 18th century, and those figures may well hold, but they have not yet been confirmed. Until they are, the tree's age is an open question. Getting there takes some planning. The nearest station, Dunbridge, is about 1.5 kilometres away, and the journey from Winchester involves a change of train.

trees.story:
The largest London plane in Britain, by Wikipedia's account, grows beside a house that began as a medieval priory. Mottisfont, in the Test valley near Romsey, was founded as an Augustinian priory in the early 13th century and turned into a country house after Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries. The plane came much later, though nobody can yet say exactly when.

It has a name of its own, the Great Plane of Mottisfont, and OpenStreetMap's mappers tag it as a landmark about 30 metres tall. Tree recorders have reported a bigger height, a vast girth and an 18th-century planting, and they may well be right, but those figures are still unconfirmed reports. Its age is an open question. If you know where the measured record lives, tell us.

The superlative, too, is worth holding loosely until a register entry backs it. What nobody disputes is the tree itself, a single crown big enough to have earned a proper name on a map, standing close to the house that grew out of the priory.

Mottisfont belongs to the National Trust and charges admission, free to members. The nearest station is Dunbridge, about 1.5 kilometres away, and from Winchester it is a day out rather than a quick hop, with a change of train on the way.
